title: Russian dissident Garry Kasparov says US warned him of danger to his life
description: An exiled Russian opposition figure living in the US says he was warned by American and Lithuanian security services that his life was in danger.Forme
body: An exiled Russian opposition figure living in the US says he was warned by American and Lithuanian security services that his life was in danger.Former chess world champion Garry Kasparov said he was one of two dissidents told to take precautions, which he had done.His comments come after the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment earlier this month charging five people who allegedly work for a network linked to the Kremlin with plotting attacks and murders in countries including the US, focusing on Russian dissidents and defectors.Kasparov wrote in his publication The Next Move that he had not been told explicitly that he and fellow Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin were considered targets, but said both had been warned about their safety.Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that it had obtained information that Kasparov, along with another Russian opposition figure, Ilya Ponomarev, had been warned about the plot over the summer by US authorities.Citing sources close to Kasparov, the paper said he had been placed under enhanced protection over the summer for the first time since he moved to the US.Kasparov wrote separately: "I will not stop and I will not hide, even if I thought it was possible to do so. "My family and I will not truly be safe as long as [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is in power in Russia - a circumstance shared by millions."Kasparov retired from competitive chess in 2005 to pursue a career in politics, founding movements that openly opposed Putin before fleeing Russia in 2013.He has not returned since. Russia classed him as a foreign agent following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and subsequently added him to a list of terrorists and extremists in 2024 - both categorisations he rejects.The other reported target, Ponomarev, was the only Russian MP who voted against the illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and later went into exile in Ukraine.He declined to confirm or deny to the Moscow Times whether he had been tipped off about the alleged plot but said the allegations marked "a new level of escalation" by Russia.A network of individuals working for the Russian intelligence services has operated since at least 2024, the US Justice Department said.It said the so-called RIS Network had been conspiring and conducting attacks and murders on Russian dissidents and defectors around the world.Five alleged members of the network had been accused of operating "as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin", Assistant Attorney General for national security John A Eisenberg said.The five people alleged to be responsible for organising the plots are Yuri Khrameev, Kirill Khrameev, Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, Yaidel Delgado Suarez and Angel Eduardo Castro.All five remain at large, the Justice Department said.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said when the indictment was unsealed that he would not comment on the charges until he had heard or seen "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts".

schema.headline: Russian dissident Garry Kasparov says US warned him of danger to his life

title: Japan raises permanent residency fees for foreigners by 20 times
description: Japan has raised fees for foreigners seeking permanent residency in the country by 20 times to 200,000 yen ($1,270; £955).Those seeking permanent resi
body: Japan has raised fees for foreigners seeking permanent residency in the country by 20 times to 200,000 yen ($1,270; £955).Those seeking permanent residency must now also meet new income, pension and Japanese-language requirements.Long lines formed outside immigration offices earlier this week as applicants sought to beat the fee hikes, with Tokyo's main immigration bureau reporting wait times of over seven hours.The fee increases are part of a series of changes to Japan's immigration policy under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, which aim to manage its rapidly growing foreign population.In July, Japan implemented a five-fold increase in visa fees for all foreigners – its first visa fee hike in 50 years. Authorities said this was meant to "reflect inflation and exchange rate fluctuations".Although immigration remains politically sensitive and restrictive in Japan, the nation's ageing population is increasingly relying on foreign workers to plug a labour shortage. Japan's foreign resident population surpassed 4.12 million at the end of 2025, marking a record 9.5% increase from the previous year. This however has led to growing anxieties over immigration and social change.Takaichi has made managing immigration one of her key priorities since she took office in October last year.In an X post days before the residency permit hikes set in, Takaichi wrote that her government recognises that "some members of the public may feel a sense of concern or unfairness" as Japan's foreign resident population grows."To address these concerns, [the government] is working to ensure that its policies toward foreign nationals are orderly, and that both Japanese citizens and foreign residents can live safely and securely," she wrote.Before the hikes, it would cost non-permanent residents in Japan 6,000 yen each time they applied to change their residency status or extend their period of stay.From 1 October, the fee varies according to the duration of stay sought – from 10,000 yen for three months or less, to 75,000 yen for five years or more.Applicants who face financial hardship or are designated as refugees would be granted discounts.Aspiring permanent residents must now also earn a stable income at or above the Japanese average. Latest data released in July puts average household income at 5.75 million yen as of 2024.Micaiah Stevens, who has been living and working in Tokyo for 10 years, was not able to compile the necessary documentation to submit his application for permanent residency before the price hike. The 37-year-old still plans to apply, but questions the new measures aimed at foreign residents."My immediate reaction was that foreigners were being treated a bit too conveniently. We're being asked to make more than the average Japanese person, pay a significantly higher fee, just to be able to work in Japan and provide taxes," he tells the BBC."There's already a significant language and cultural barrier that prevents some talent from coming over. This just doesn't strike me as a plan that was thought out to the long term."From April next year, permanent residency applicants will face even tighter requirements, including basic Japanese language proficiency. This has led to a surge in enrollments at Japanese language schools as well as people signing up to take the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, local media reported.Applicants' expected pension benefits must also be equivalent to that of someone who has enrolled into the employee pension system for 30 years, although the value of one's financial assets can be considered if their expected pension benefits fall short.

schema.headline: Japan raises permanent residency fees for foreigners by 20 times

title: Kanye West's Russia shows cancelled after stadium row
description: Russia was invaded by the Nazis in World War Two, and the country's Foreign Ministry spokeswoman was among those who criticised the planned shows.Mari
body: Russia was invaded by the Nazis in World War Two, and the country's Foreign Ministry spokeswoman was among those who criticised the planned shows.Maria Zakharova said they were unacceptable and pointed out West's "glorification" of Hitler.In 2025 West started selling swastika T-shirts and released a song called Heil Hitler. Pro-war bloggers in Russia also questioned whether the country should be hosting an American artist while the US provided financial and military support for Ukraine.West is yet to comment publicly on the cancellation.His first major concert in the US for more than five years was held in Los Angeles in April, and he has since played in countries including Spain, Portugal and the Netherlands.However, his Russian shows aren't the only gigs to have been cancelled.Last summer West was set to headline London's Wireless Festival but was barred from entering the UK, forcing organisers to cancel the whole event.West shows were also cancelled in Poland, Italy and France.

schema.headline: Kanye West's Russia shows cancelled after stadium row

title: Flight attacker 'underwent Islamist radical indoctrination', Netanyahu says
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesByOlivia IrelandIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesByOlivia IrelandIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu also said it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".Figure caption, Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutesThe co-pilot is currently being questioned in Saudi Arabia, where the plane made an emergency landing. However UAE officials say they have jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal that's not a question"."And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think ... that'll give us a pretty good clue but again I don't make final conclusions yet but that's the indications we have now." The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".The attacker was arrested in Saudi Arabia and is expected to be transferred to the UAE, Netanyahu said.Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero". India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well". Image source, Embassy of India in IsraelImage caption, The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at  Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers. The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

schema.headline: Flight attacker 'underwent Islamist radical indoctrination', Netanyahu says

title: Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials
description: The family of a woman who was killed by an immigration agent in Minneapolis in January has announced two lawsuits against the US government and member
body: The family of a woman who was killed by an immigration agent in Minneapolis in January has announced two lawsuits against the US government and members of the Trump administration.Renee Good, a US citizen, was shot to death by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during a major immigration sweep. Millions watched the video recorded of her killing and residents of the Minnesota city took to the streets to protest.One lawsuit blames the government for her death, claiming the operation created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence",  a lawyer for the family said.The BBC has contacted the White House and Department of Homeland Security (DHS).The lawsuits were brought by Good's brother, Brent Ganger, and her partner, Becca Good. Speaking publicly for the first time since the shooting, Becca Good told a news conference on the lawsuits on Thursday: "The whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed.""We were all robbed," she said as she described how the shooting affected their three children.In one of the lawsuits, the family accuses the government of "battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused Renee's death".It cites the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows citizens to sue the government for personal injury, death, or property damage caused by the negligence of federal employees.The second lawsuit targets ICE officer Jonathan Ross, who shot Good, as well as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House border chief Tom Homan and others, alleging a "conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials, federal immigration enforcement agents, and private actors"."Our government has become a grave and mortal threat to its own citizens," the family's lawyer, Antonio Romanucci said at the news conference.Trump initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, willfully, and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents sometimes are "going to make a mistake".Good was a 37-year-old mother of three who had just moved to the city. She was shot on 7 January in a traffic stop, which immigration authorities said occurred after she made "an attempt to kill or cause bodily harm to agents". Witnesses disputed that she was attempting to attack officers.Her death sparked nationwide protests that intensified after another Minneapolis resident, Alex Pretti, was killed by immigration agents on 24 January.  Weeks later, hundreds of federal agents were withdrawn from the city and the official in charge of the operation, Greg Bovino, was removed from his post. Granger, Good's brother, said at Thursday's news conference that "since her death no meaningful change has occurred"."Our family is waiting and we will wait no longer," he said.At least 10 people have been killed in encounters with immigration officers during Trump's second term, which began in January 2025, according to the Associated Press news agency.

schema.headline: Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials

title: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss
description: Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.More than
body: Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed. But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting. Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear."It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer."At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear."Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion."But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.

schema.headline: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss

title: Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide
description: Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studyi
body: Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studying conditions.Blazes were reported at two high schools in Nantes, western France, while another was filmed engulfing the entrance to another in the northern city of Rouen.Students are protesting about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined the demonstrations on Thursday, citing similar demands.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu held a crisis meeting on Thursday to discuss the unrest. The government said afterwards that the student-led demonstrations had descended into "urban violence".Both fires in Nantes spread after a bin was set alight. The blaze at the Nelson Mandela high school, in the city centre, then spread to the front of the building, damaging the entrance hall.In the southern city of Marseille, staff at Victor Hugo high school were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.While in the north, a headteacher at Degrugillier high school, in the village of Auchel, was injured in the ear by a wayward firework.The blockades and protests at French lycées - for 15-18 year olds and equivalent to sixth forms in the UK or high schools in the US - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.French media report 625 people were arrested on Wednesday alone while 83 police officers were injured. More than 600 arrests had been made by midday on Thursday,  excluding Paris, broadcaster ICI reports. At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris.On Thursday, public transport services in Marseille and Strasbourg were halted due vandalism, threats of violence and to hinder protesters from moving around.Seventeen-year-old Raphael took part in protests outside a school in Strasbourg, where barriers were used to obstruct nearby tram tracks. He voiced his frustration at his school's facilities in an interview with news agency AFP, saying some rooms had leaks and that there were not enough toilets."The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There's zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors," Raphael said.While France's next general election is still months away, the protests and how French authorities are responding to them has been heavily politicised.The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for igniting protests, which are being organised by a union representing lycée students.Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of a Parisian suburb and member of the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party defended earlier remarks in which he said violence could be legitimate in some cases - referencing cases in which protesters had allegedly been shot at while not wearing helmets or bulletproof vests.LFI leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, meanwhile, stressed he was in favour of non-violent protests, while arguing that blaming the left would not solve the issues motivating the demonstrations.Earlier, leader of the hard-right National Rally Marine Le Pen said: "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organized by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise."The presidential candidate called for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.Left-wing mayor of Marseille Benoît Payan condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city. While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves in a calm fashion, he said.Eric Ciotti, the Republicans mayor of Nice, said the parents of those found to have damaged school property should be made to pay for the repairs.

schema.headline: Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide

title: Addis Ababa explosions: Blasts heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned
description: Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital, some in the area of the military headquarters in the west and another in the south of the city,
body: Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital, some in the area of the military headquarters in the west and another in the south of the city, residents and diplomatic sources say.The blasts came hours after drone flights were banned over Addis Ababa and a week after fighting erupted in the north between the army and a newly launched alliance of armed groups including forces from the Tigray region.A source linked to the opposition fighters told the Reuters news agency they were behind what they said were drone strikes."It was very loud. It was strong enough to set off car alarms," a resident in a southern area of the city, near the base of the secret service, told BBC Amharic.He estimated that he heard the explosion in the Gotera neighbourhood some time around 00:30 local time (21:30 GMT).Another resident told the BBC that he and his friends were playing games when they heard an explosion.He lives in the western suburb of Torhayloch, a neighbourhood close to the military headquarters.There were no official reports confirming the cause of the explosions, the exact locations affected or whether there were any casualties or damage.The office of Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, the defence ministry as well as the federal and Addis Ababa police have not responded to BBC requests for comment.Meanwhile, Ethiopia's foreign ministry has said it is closing its embassy in neighbouring Eritrea and expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats "for involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security".Earlier, in a BBC interview, Eritrea's government denied that it was backing the new rebel alliance.Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).They both accuse each other of violating a 2022 peace deal that ended a brutal two-year civil war, which according to an Africa Union mediator is estimated to have cost 600,000 lives.Last month, seven armed movements, including the TPLF and an Amhara militia known as Fano, formed an alliance with the stated aim of removing the government in Addis Ababa.There is disagreement over which side started the latest fighting.The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region.The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas. It is difficult to verify what is happening on the ground and access to the internet and the main telecoms service provider in Tigray have also been cut.Within Tigray, the national army and a pro-government militia appear to be advancing towards the region's main city of Mekelle.In the southern Tigrayan town of Alamata, a medic told the BBC on Wednesday that 52 civilians had died in three days of heavy fighting.The TPLF is also reported to be fighting in neighbouring Afar region, a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports.A humanitarian source has estimated that tens of thousands have fled their homes in Afar, according to the AFP news agency.Fighting around Lalibela in the Amhara region, a Unesco world heritage site where foreign tourists have been stranded for more than a week, has involved the national army and Fano fighters, now allied to the TPLF.The government has accused neighbouring Eritrea of backing these groups.One pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers were involved on the front lines.But in a rare response to the BBC from Eritrea's government, Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel dismissed the allegations.He accused Ethiopia's ruling Prosperity Party (PP) of seeking external scapegoats for the country's mounting challenges."The PP regime has made it a habit to apportion blame to its neighbours in order to deflect attention from the myriad internal conflicts that it is fomenting in various parts of the country," he told BBC Tigrinya.Eritrea was a key ally of Ethiopia during the Tigray war, fighting against the TPLF.But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports.Ethiopia lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993.Abiy has even hinted at taking the port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - by force as he sees direct access to the sea as important for Ethiopia's long-term future and economic prosperity.As concerns over security mount in Ethiopia, the country's National Intelligence and Security Service (Niss) announced on Wednesday that it was imposing an indefinite ban on drone flights in Addis Ababa and surrounding areas.The agency said it would not issue permits for drone operations and warned that legal action would be taken against anyone flying drones in restricted areas.Niss said the measure was necessary to protect national leaders, critical infrastructure and major public events.

schema.headline: Addis Ababa explosions: Blasts heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned

title: Tennessee halts executions after Christa Pike survives two lethal injection attempts
description: Executions in Tennessee have been halted for the rest of the year, Governor Bill Lee has said, after two attempts to execute death row inmate Christa
body: Executions in Tennessee have been halted for the rest of the year, Governor Bill Lee has said, after two attempts to execute death row inmate Christa Pike by lethal injection failed.Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Lee said he was "highly disappointed" about the botched execution, which he called one of the state's "most serious responsibilities". He has ordered an independent review.Tennessee prison officials on Wednesday attempted to administer two lethal doses of pentobarbital to Pike but she survived and was taken to hospital. Her medical condition is unclear. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer.Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in Tennessee for over 200 years. Lee said on Thursday the investigation into Pike's botched execution "will be thorough", adding that "it's going to take time"."There are a lot of questions," Lee said. "The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered, and that's what this investigation is for." Lee has not made clear who will conduct the independent review of the state's execution procedures. His order to pause all executions will overlap with the planned 3 December execution of convicted murderer Gary Sutton.In court filings, Pike's lawyers said she needed "life-saving measures" after her botched execution. The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the execution, issued a statement defending its handling of the case. It said in a statement that it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office"."The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening."Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital, as per state protocol when the first attempt fails, but was still alive afterwards, according to court filings."This execution is causing Ms Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of his right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment," her lawyers said.The Tennessee attorney general's office said in a statement that it agreed with the decision to call for an investigation, adding: "We need to know what happened."Pike's attempted execution proceeded after multiple last-minute legal challenges by her lawyers had failed, overturned in the final hour by the US Supreme Court.Slemmer's mother May Martinez, who was among those who wanted the execution to take place and who travelled to Tennessee to witness it, told NBC News after the botched attempt that "it was a mess".US Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is running for Tennessee governor, described the situation as "tragic"."While there should be a thorough review of what happened and why the process failed, the answer is simple: bring back the electric chair," Blackburn said.Democrat Jerri Green, Blackburn's opponent, criticised her for wanting to "bring back one of the most cruel forms of capital punishment". "As governor, I would put a moratorium on all future executions," Green said on X.This is the second time in 2026 Tennessee officials attempted and failed to execute a prisoner. In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers was called off after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug. Carruthers was given a one-year reprieve.With additional reporting by Stephanie Hegarty, World Service correspondent

schema.headline: Tennessee halts executions after Christa Pike survives two lethal injection attempts

title: Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
description: A man has described how he hugged and reassured his two young children as their plane suddenly descended after one pilot stabbed the other in an attem
body: A man has described how he hugged and reassured his two young children as their plane suddenly descended after one pilot stabbed the other in an attempt to seize control of the flight.A Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes around two hours into its journey from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered him and retook control to land safely.Adam Polovincik told BBC Newshour that he hugged his six-year-old son and three-year-old daughter "really hard" and tried to stay calm for them as the attack unfolded.He praised the pilot who was stabbed and passengers who fought off and subdued the attacker, saying they were "true heroes".The stabbed pilot is in a stable condition in hospital, while the alleged attacker has been arrested.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to say whether Iran was involved in the attack, but that the alleged attacker had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".Polovincik, who was sitting in aisle 13, was flying home with his wife and children after an "amazing" holiday in Singapore and Thailand. He said there had been a "huge degree of panic" on the plane as there was a "very, very, very sharp decrease in height". He thought at first that this was simply because of an air pocket, but "it took a lot of time, almost a minute".Everyone who had not been seated fell to the floor, the 40-year-old said. "After a couple of seconds, we started to hear screams. 'There is blood, there is stabbing, we need help'," Polovincik said."At the end of the day, you understand very, very quickly that literally there is nothing that you can do at this point in time," he said.Polovincik, a performance marketing analyst, said he tried to "be cool" for his children."You just tell them, yeah, everything's going to be all right. It's just a malfunction in the aeroplane, there is a crew under control, the passengers are helping them, [you] hug them really hard and try to keep your face so it doesn't look very panicked, try to keep your tone of voice."But he said there was naturally a "high degree of panic" on the flight.There were lots of families with children on the plane because the flight took place towards the end of a Jewish holiday period.After about 10 to 15 minutes, he said a passenger in the cockpit told them the incident was "under control" and other staff were flying the plane. In a video released by Netanyahu's office, passenger Yaniv Hayun described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him out of the cockpit before other passengers helped pin him down.Two other pilots who were onboard the flight then took over the controls and safely landed the plane, which had been carrying more than 150 passengers.Polovincik said: "After they told us that the situation is, again, 'under control', then it was a bit harder to tell the kids that it's malfunctioned because people start to walk around the aeroplane covered with blood."Polovincik was praised Indian pilot, Capt Smit Machchhar, who fought off his attacker and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing passengers to step in."Without him opening the door, we're probably not speaking here right now," he said, adding that he "can't even start saying our gratitude for this human being".Polovincik said that, although he was not religious, he could not escape "the feeling that it was the hand of God yesterday" that had put "the pieces on the board in the way that they did"."It's remarkable."After the situation onboard was brought under control, the flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia, where Polovincik stressed the passengers, who were almost all Israeli, were treated well. "They brought us water and food and coffee and even sweets for the kids - even though we don't have any diplomatic relationship between Israel and Saudi Arabia," he said.The alleged attacker, who was arrested in Saudi Arabia, is expected to be transferred to the United Arab Emirates, from where the plane departed, Netanyahu told Fox News.The passengers were taken to Tel Aviv on another flight later on Wednesday and were greeted at the airport by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.Polovincik said it had been "such a terrible ending" to an amazing family trip and that it would take some time for his family to come to terms with what had occurred.

schema.headline: Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack

title: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing
description: Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the pla
body: Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the plane, while others described the "terrifying" moment they thought they would die.Appearing in a bloodstained shirt after the ordeal, Yaniv Hayun told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he realised something was wrong when the aircraft suddenly dropped. The plane, en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv, plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes."Someone screamed... the light went out," Hayun said in a video posted by the prime minister on social media.He and others tried to push open the cockpit door, but the pilot who had been stabbed was very close to it, so it was hard to open. Before he collapsed, the injured pilot managed to open the door.When Hayun and another man entered the cockpit, he said he saw one pilot down and the attacker on the instruments, between the two seats, "trying to destroy the instruments in order to...disable the plane"."I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside," Hayun said."We pulled him out; it was a matter of seconds. I called out to the Israeli guys with us on the plane - I called them, and two other guys came over to me... we pinned [the attacker] down to keep him secure."The Flydubai flight eventually landed at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, and the passengers were later taken to Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport on a repatriation aircraft.They were greeted by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags."Thank God I'm alive," passenger Haim Lazarovich told journalists, adding that "the most terrifying moment in this flight was when the pilot loses control".Oran Choen, an 18-year-old passenger, described the incident as "a very tough moment"."Maybe it was five minutes, but it feels like hell - I heard my brother behind me scream that we was going to die," he added.A paramedic from Israel's ambulance service later told the BBC that a number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane". The stabbed pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, was taken to hospital but is in stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia. Netanyahu praised Machchhar as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery".The attacker was arrested and is being questioned by Saudi authorities. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack". No official motive for the incident or further information has been given.US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.

schema.headline: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing

title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
description: Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official nation
body: Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry.The US president wants AI to be called "super intelligence" - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites.Register.si spokeswoman Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%.She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September."The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk.Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to just Trump's comments.She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.One possible explanation for the purchases is a practice in which people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age" on Tuesday.He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence", and to no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online, external however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath Trump's signature.Correction 1 October:  An earlier version of this article referred to cyber-squatting, whereby people register domain names in bad faith with the intent to profit. We cited as an example the registration of men.com by Rick Schwartz. The article was amended to delete the reference to cyber-squatting and make clear simply registering domain names as an investment in the hope they will increase in value, as happened with men.com, is a legitimate business activity.

schema.headline: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names

title: Aliko Dangote launches Kenya oil refinery amid land protest in Lamu
description: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya's President William Ruto have broken ground on a $16bn (£12bn) oil refinery in Lamu, on Kenya's northern
body: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya's President William Ruto have broken ground on a $16bn (£12bn) oil refinery in Lamu, on Kenya's northern coast.Upon completion, the refinery is expected to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil a day, making it East Africa's largest industrial project by capacity. Ahead of the launch, some local residents took to the streets to demand more compensation for land used for the refinery.Speaking to the BBC, Dangote, Africa's richest man, dismissed the protests as games played by local marketers and international players, insisting the refinery would go ahead and would be ready by 2030 as planned.The ground-breaking was also attended by the leaders of Uganda, Ethiopia, Togo and Benin.Dangote has offered regional governments a combined 30% stake in the refinery, according to Reuters news agency."This is Africa coming together to build Africa. Today we are not simply breaking ground for a refinery, we're breaking ground for a new chapter in Africa's industrial journey to a brighter future," Dangote said as he launched the project."Lekki [his Nigerian refinery] proved that it can be done, Lamu must prove that it can be repeated."President Ruto made a similar point, saying: "It is a declaration that Africa has entered a new age in which we will increasingly finance, build, process and add value here at home."The refinery is set to become the only one in East Africa and is Kenya's largest infrastructure project since independence, surpassing the $5.1bn (£3.9bn) Standard Gauge Railway.In his interview with the BBC's Focus on Africa programme, Dangote disputed the compensation claims and said the company took only the portion of land it needed from what the government made available."To come and say some people are demonstrating, demonstrating about what? Have you ever seen people demonstrating against themselves in terms of development?" he asked, indicating he was not fazed by the protests.Walid Ali, the co-founder of the Save Lamu campaign group, told the BBC that they are concerned about the environmental impact the project could have on the local community."We are asking for the findings from the environmental impact assessment so that we can see what mitigation measures are being proposed," Ali said. "This is not the first project where we have seen environmental concerns being overlooked," he added.A group of 133 Lamu residents has approached Kenya's High Court in a bid to stop the construction work.As a result, activities such as excavation and construction on the disputed land are restricted until the next court hearing on 14 October.At the height of construction, Dangote said the refinery would create 60,000 jobs, with the benefits extending beyond those employed directly by the project. "Are we going to bring robots? Of course, the people will benefit," he said.Critics have questioned the decision to build the refinery in Kenya, which is not an oil-producing country. Others have suggested Tanzania or Uganda, both of which are moving towards oil exports through the East African Crude Oil Pipeline. But Kenya's Energy and Petroleum Minister Opiyo Wandayi told the BBC that the refinery's location did not mean it would rely on oil from the region. "Refineries get crude oil from the market. And the market is open," he said.Dangote made a similar point, citing Singapore as an example. "Singapore doesn't produce a single drop of oil, yet they have a lot of refineries," Dangote said.The refinery will also include a 1,000-megawatt power plant. Dangote sees reliable electricity as a critical constraint on industrialisation across Africa, particularly in mineral-rich countries that still export raw materials rather than processing them locally.He has about $50bn (£38bn) worth of projects in the pipeline, including plans to develop 10,000 megawatts of power generation capacity across Africa by 2030, with the potential to double that depending on demand.In Lamu, the new power plant is designed to support Dangote's operations as well as other industries expected to set up in the area."The power is there and what you do is what we call plug and play," he said.Kenya has relatively high fuel prices, raising expectations that greater refining capacity could eventually help bring down pump prices. However, the price of crude oil, the main raw material for fuel, set by international markets, remains a major factor in what consumers pay at the pump.The Lamu refinery is Dangote's largest proposed investment outside Nigeria. His refinery in Nigeria also has a processing capacity of 700,000 barrels a day. Dangote plans to double that capacity after floating 4.1 million ordinary shares to raise up to $2.1bn earlier this month.

schema.headline: Aliko Dangote launches Kenya oil refinery amid land protest in Lamu

title: ‘Super Intelligence’: Three takeaways from Trump's tech summit
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Trump met top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday to discuss AIByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterUS President D
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Trump met top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday to discuss AIByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterUS President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age".The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry.The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity.Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House.1. AI 'self-regulation' pactTrump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting.The president said the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.Under the agreement, which Trump posted online, external, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues.They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang."It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president."Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Trump with top tech leaders at the White House on TuesdayTrump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board.Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended, calling the meeting a "historic conversation".Amodei called it a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins".But not all technology experts are impressed with the accord.Nanyang Technological University AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said the pact shows "emerging consensus" but does not address whether AI developers should be held accountable for incidents.It is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations around the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatherall from the University of Sydney.The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are for any breaches, Weatherall said."The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added.Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight over the technology.On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns.The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation.Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said self-regulation could mean that companies set "only minimal safeguards".The agreement inspires "very little confidence" as recent incidents of AI going rogue suggest companies have been undisciplined in their approach, she added.2. Doubling down on data centresTrump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI.The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the US over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on communities.Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November.A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News, external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas.Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres. "These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters.The president previously said on social media that the only reason communities should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor".Huang, whose company produces computer chips essential for running AI, said after the meeting that data centres should be called "super intelligence factories".These facilities are "reindustrialising the United States", creating jobs across the economy, he added.3. It's now 'Super Intelligence' Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said."As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said.Image source, EPAImage caption, Trump spoke to the media alongside tech executives after the summitDuring an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake".Some tech leaders, including Zuckerberg and Musk, and other people close to the president have already started to use the term.With tech leaders adopting the term, the US "may well be able to set the nomenclature," Paterson said.But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that they thought the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems.

schema.headline: ‘Super Intelligence’: Three takeaways from Trump's tech summit

title: Tiny image sparks big backlash in Nikon photo contest
description: The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made
body: The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI.Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years.The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease.Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules.In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn, external, he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest."AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said. Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself.He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images".But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big.Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere".Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated.Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real.Nikon said Xu was "respectfully complying" with its investigation and had provided it with additional technical documents.Dr Patrick Hickey, who came fifth in the 2026 Small World contest, said the recognition the award represents means more than the $3,000 (£2,250) prize itself."If you spend a lot of your time in a dark room looking down a microscope, it's really nice to be able to show people and to show the public," he said."There's an interesting fusion between science and art, and a lot of the images that scientists are making have some very abstract and artistic qualities to them."Hickey said it would be unfair on other entrants if it turned out the winning video was unfairly altered by AI."There's a specific set of rules in the contest, and one of them was quite clearly that you couldn't use generative AI to produce things, and the other was obviously that it has to be taken under a microscope," he said.So far, Nikon is standing by its procedures but it said there would be an update soon."At this time, we don't see that any rules were violated," it said in a statement.

schema.headline: Tiny image sparks big backlash in Nikon photo contest
